Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Kenya predominantly use paper-based systems for recording criminal cases and complaints, including manual Occurrence Books (OB), P3 medical forms, and paper dockets. These are later aggregated or digitized at higher levels, as evidenced by World Bank digitization of 17,000 paper crash reports from Nairobi stations. Digital initiatives like Digital OB (piloted/launched in urban stations such as Kasarani 2019 and Eldoret 2026) and NPSIMS (unified platform presented 2025) exist, but rollout depends on connectivity assessments, explicitly noting challenges in rural areas. A 2021 SRIC pilot digitized arms registers (not cases) in rural ASAL counties (Baringo, Samburu, etc.), confirming manual records pre-pilot. Recent plans (2025 digital services by April, online reporting) remain aspirational with infrastructure gaps (power, internet, training). No evidence majority rural facilities use digital at point-of-service; isolated pilots indicate score 1 (entirely paper), conservatively, due to thin rural-specific evidence amid urban-focused rollouts.

The cited World Bank source (eCrash pilot digitising ~17,000 historical paper crash reports, 2012-2021, Nairobi) was fetched and verified but concerns higher-level/retrospective digitisation rather than facility point-of-service capture, so per the metadata guidance it does not itself support a higher score. Fresh 2025-2026 searches confirm a national Digital Occurrence Book (OB)/NPSIMS rollout is under way but remains behind schedule (an April 2025 completion target was missed; as of May 2026 the Inspector-General still describes the digital system as '3-4 months away'), digital OB pilots are running only in named urban/peri-urban stations (e.g. Eldoret Central, Langas), and rural network-connectivity investment (an estimated KES 11 billion request made in March 2025) remains unfunded. Rural stations therefore remain paper-based at point of service. Score confirmed at 1.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Kenya record cases and complaints using paper-based Occurrence Books, P3 medical forms and paper dockets at the point of service. A national Digital Occurrence Book (Digital OB) and the National Police Service Information Management System (NPSIMS) are being rolled out, with pilots running in selected urban and peri-urban stations (for example Eldoret Central, Langas, Sukunanga, Ainabtich and Kamkunji), but nationwide completion has repeatedly slipped past announced targets and network-connectivity investment for rural stations (an estimated KES 11 billion request) remains largely unfunded. Data capture in rural stations therefore remains entirely paper-based at the point of service, with digitisation occurring later through central aggregation or urban pilot programmes.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Kenya predominantly use paper registers for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes at the point of service. National systems like NEMIS/KEMIS exist for aggregate reporting, but rural schools lack the infrastructure (electricity, internet, computers) and trained staff for routine digital entry—data is likely collected manually and submitted to district offices for digitization. Pilots and donor projects provide isolated digital tools (e.g., solar labs), but these do not represent the majority. Key barriers include poor connectivity, unreliable power, low teacher digital literacy, and high student-teacher ratios. National policies push EMIS adoption, but rural reality lags far behind, with studies showing low ICT readiness even in 2020s. Score 2 reflects predominant paper with some digital aggregation/pilots.

revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Kenya record attendance, enrolment and learning outcomes chiefly on paper registers at the point of service. The Ministry of Education is transitioning from NEMIS to the Kenya Education Management Information System (KEMIS), which became mandatory for capitation disbursement from June 2026 and is being extended to school level through a network of 'KEMIS Champion Teachers' nominated in May 2026, alongside periodic digital data-collection exercises such as the 2024 school census using a mobile data-capture app. Rural schools generally lack reliable electricity, internet and computing equipment for routine day-to-day digital data entry, and isolated digital pilots (for example an attendance-tracking application trialled in Baringo) have not yet become the norm. The overall picture is one of predominantly paper-based record-keeping with meaningful and growing digital reporting and administrative layers.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary clinics in Kenya predominantly use paper registers for patient data recording, with dual documentation alongside digital systems where available. EMRs like KenyaEMR (KeEMR) cover ~91-93% of facilities including rural level 2/3 dispensaries and health centers (e.g., Homa Bay County survey of 112 facilities, 79% rural), but are mainly for HIV management, donor-driven, and fragmented (9-10 systems co-existing). General care relies on paper; data aggregated monthly into DHIS2 by HRIOs, not entered digitally at POC routinely. Pilots like ScanForm (AI paper digitization, 24% facilities) and AfyaEHMS exist but isolated. Barriers: poor internet/power, interoperability lack, training gaps, staff turnover. National policies (Digital Health Act 2023, eHealth Strategy) aim for integrated systems, but rural reality lags due to infra disparities, uneven county implementation—some manual, policy ambition unmet at POC (Homa Bay study; Policy Brief; DHIS2 perceptions).

revision_notes: Original score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed. The cited PMC sources could not be fetched directly (reCAPTCHA-blocked) but are consistent with independently verified evidence: a Central Kenya thesis (Kiambu, Murang'a, Kirinyaga, Nyeri, Nyandarua counties) confirms all HIV comprehensive care clinics use a hybrid of paper and KenyaEMR, with none having gone fully paperless; a Kiambu County study confirms 100% of surveyed maternal/child health facilities recorded data manually on paper registers prior to a small DHIS2 pilot. The Human Rights/CIPESA policy brief (March 2025) was fetched and verified and supports ongoing infrastructure and rural disparities in health digitalisation. Fresh searches found that Balambala Sub-County Hospital (Garissa) was announced in August 2025 as Kenya's first fully digitised rural hospital, and that the Ministry of Health reports 93% of public facilities as 'digitally transformed' for Social Health Authority (SHA) HMIS purposes by June 2026 - this appears to relate primarily to SHA billing/claims onboarding rather than full clinical point-of-care digitisation, so does not change the facility-level record-capture assessment. Score confirmed at 2.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Kenya predominantly document patient care using paper registers (for example MOH 405, 406, 333 and 511 forms for antenatal, postnatal, maternity and child welfare services) at the point of service, while parallel digital systems are used mainly for HIV care management (KenyaEMR, covering an estimated 91-93% of facilities including many rural dispensaries and health centres) and for billing and claims under the Social Health Authority (SHA) Health Management Information System, whose rollout has accelerated markedly during 2025-2026. Studies of HIV comprehensive care clinics find that all sites continue to run paper registers alongside electronic records, with none having achieved a fully paperless clinical workflow. Balambala Sub-County Hospital in Garissa was announced in August 2025 as Kenya's first fully digitised rural hospital, indicating that full facility-level digitisation remains the exception rather than the rule among rural clinics. Overall, the evidence points to a hybrid model in which paper remains the primary medium for routine clinical documentation, supplemented by significant and expanding digital systems for specific programmes and administrative functions.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: In rural Kenya, birth registration primarily occurs at sub-locations manned by Assistant Chiefs (10,666 total) or rural health facilities via paper Form B1, completed manually in duplicate. The informant receives the original notification slip, while duplicates are batched and sent to Civil Registration Offices (CROs) for verification and entry into registers. Rural residents often travel 5-10 km (1-4 hours on foot) to access these points. Post-collection, sub-county registrars create Excel summaries from paper registers and transmit electronically to national CRS, but point-of-service remains paper-based. Digital efforts include: CRVSS piloted in some counties (not scaled due to resources); historical digitization of 46M records; IPRS for national linkage; hospital digital pilots (e.g., Estonia-supported e-birth registration, 2025—not rural-focused); small-scale mobile pilots (e.g., WHO MoVE-IT, Finnish/Nokia 2008-2012). Low rural completeness (e.g., ASAL counties <20%) reflects access barriers, insecurity, and lack of digital tools at RAs. Barriers: poor connectivity/electricity, low capacity among rural agents, backlogs, distance. National ambitions (e.g., 2018-2023 strategy, eCitizen integration) outpace rural rollout, where paper dominates point-of-service with digital limited to pilots/aggregation. Score 2: Predominantly paper; digital in isolated pilots/central reporting.UNECA CRVS Kenya Snapshot; Kenya Vital Statistics Report 2022; UNECA Digitalization CRVS Africa

revision_notes: Original score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed. The UNECA CRVS Kenya Snapshot was fetched and verified, describing the paper Form B1/D1-based registration process via Assistant Chiefs and health facilities. The cited 2022 KNBS Vital Statistics Report could not be fetched directly (crawl timeout), but the equivalent 2023 KNBS Vital Statistics Report was located and confirms the same paper-based registration process and a 2023 national birth registration completeness of 77.1%. Fresh 2025-2026 searches found a 2024 amendment to the Births and Deaths Registration Rules requiring registers to be kept in loose-leaf and electronic form, a digital birth e-notification pilot launched from around April 2026 (Nairobi Hospital only) linked to the Maisha Namba identity system, and training of chiefs and registration assistants on the Unique Personal Identifier (UPI) system (e.g. in Gucha, Kisii County), alongside an explicit acknowledgement by the Civil Registration Service Secretary in March 2026 that the current system 'relies heavily on paper-based processes'. This confirms rural point-of-service registration remains predominantly paper, with digital elements limited to central systems, training initiatives and early-stage urban pilots. Score confirmed at 2.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Kenya register vital events chiefly on paper. Registration agents - Assistant Chiefs (for home events) or health facility staff (for facility births and deaths) - complete Form B1/D1 in duplicate, retain the original locally and forward duplicates to the sub-county Civil Registration Office for verification and manual entry, with monthly compilation feeding national statistics; birth registration completeness stood at 77.1% nationally in 2023. A 2024 amendment to the Births and Deaths Registration Rules requires registers to be kept in loose-leaf and electronic form, and the government began piloting a digital birth e-notification system linking hospitals to the Maisha Namba identity platform from around April 2026, alongside training of rural chiefs and registration assistants on the Unique Personal Identifier (UPI) system. The e-notification pilot has so far only been implemented at Nairobi Hospital, and the Civil Registration Service leadership itself describes the underlying legal framework as continuing to rely heavily on paper-based processes. Point-of-service registration in rural offices therefore remains predominantly paper-based, with digital elements confined to central aggregation, training initiatives and early-stage urban pilots.
